news.title: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
news.summary_raw: AI is forcing companies to patch their systems faster as attackers race to exploit newly discovered vulnerabilities. Welcome to internet outage hell.
news.source_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.
So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.
AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.
Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”
External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.
“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of t
news.summary: Recent high-profile outages at Microsoft 365, Apple, and the NSA highlight how AI‑accelerated vulnerability discovery is stressing patch management workflows. The incidents underscore the need for IT teams to streamline and automate patch deployment to keep pace with rapid exploitation.
news.enterprise_use: Check your organization’s patch management schedule this week and enable automated vulnerability scanning in your endpoint security platform—e.g., CrowdStrike or Microsoft Defender. Failure to act promptly could leave critical systems exposed to newly discovered bugs that attackers exploit faster than traditional patch cycles. The most affected tool here is your Microsoft 365 and Azure AD environment, which requires immediate attention to avoid further outages.

news.title: RCE in Gnupg
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://lists.gnupg.org/pipermail/gnupg-announce/2026q4/000517.html
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50587208
Points: 112
# Comments: 35
news.source_text:
[Announce] GnuPG Security Advisory for GPGME (T8557,CVE-2026-129975)
    Werner Koch 
    wk at gnupg.org
       
    Fri Nov 20 19:01:51 CET 2026
    
    
  
Hello!
We are pleased to announce the availability of a new GPGME release:
version 2.3.1.  This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in
all prior versions.  We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and
GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME.
Description
===========
By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is
possible to trigger a double free.  This double free can be used
exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data.
Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't
be ruled out.  Thus an immediate update is highly suggested.
Our internal ID is T8557 (https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557)
The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975.
This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed
by GitLab on 2026-11-12.  Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated
disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier
and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20.
The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the
status lines and key listings from gpg.  Initially a buffer of 1024
bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required.  When
reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but
it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the
function.  Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or
other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to
the freed memory.  Eventually the context is released and the memory
freed a second time.  Due to other allocations in between the common
double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered.
Impact
======
All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared
libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected.  Examples of software
using GPGME are
 - Gpg4win
 - GnuPG Desktop
 - GnuPG VS-Desktop
 - Most mail clients
 - Many XMPP clients
 - Samba
 - Flatpack
Solution
========
Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1.  If you need a
DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version.
For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME
2.3.1.
If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME
version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to
very old versions.
There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT.
Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19)
================================================
         [compared to version 2.2.0]
 * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM.
   Add mappings for algos used bei backends.   [rMa85fa49236]
 * Fix a double free in the status line read code.
   [T8557,CVE-2026-129975]
 * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release:
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
news.summary: A critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-129975) has been discovered in GPGME, the library used by GnuPG and related tools. A patch is released in version 2.3.1, and immediate update is strongly advised.
news.enterprise_use: Go to your system’s package manager and upgrade GPGME to 2.3.1 or install the updated Gpg4win package within the next week. Failure to apply the patch could expose your email, XMPP, or Samba services to RCE attacks, compromising data integrity and confidentiality. The most affected tools in your stack are mail clients and any custom applications that embed GPGME for encryption.

news.title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
news.source_text:
Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.
Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!
We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.
This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.
What is new with Inkling 2 Mini?
Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.
Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.
The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.
Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.
- Each six-layer block has five sliding-window layers and one full-attention layer. The local window holds up to 1,024 tokens.
- Attention uses 24 query heads and eight KV heads. It uses learned relative position logits, a learned sink, and an output gate. Full-attention layers use dynamic key and value convolutions.
- The router selects eight of 128 SwiGLU experts for each token. It normalizes the selected scores and scales the weights by 8.
-
news.summary: Hugging Face releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26B parameter multimodal mixture-of-experts model optimized for local deployment with 1M-token context and image/text inputs. The model uses looped layers to boost effective depth while keeping memory footprint low, making it a candidate for on-prem AI workloads.
news.enterprise_use: Watch the release over the next month to evaluate whether Inkling 2 Mini could replace or supplement existing local inference pipelines, such as those in data centers or on edge devices. It may reduce reliance on cloud APIs and lower latency for image‑text processing.

news.title: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: http://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50586292
Points: 118
# Comments: 33
news.source_text:
An AI coding agent for DOS.
  It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.
A (real) human’s note:
Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age.
It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.
I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects.
From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier.
Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware?
And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent?
I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box.
As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle.
Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the
files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and
looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and
picks up where it left off.
The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that
speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the
streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk.
The 8088 does everything but TLS.
Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API.
One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running.
The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness c
news.summary: ClawDOS is an AI coding agent that runs on vintage IBM PC hardware, leveraging the Claude API to generate, compile, and execute code within the constraints of a 4.77 MHz 8088 processor and DOS. The project demonstrates pushing modern AI capabilities onto obsolete hardware for experimental and nostalgic purposes.
news.enterprise_use: This development has no direct impact on current enterprise IT stacks, so no immediate action is required.

news.title: How Sumitomo Life’s leaders helped teams adopt ChatGPT Enterprise
news.summary_raw: Sumitomo Life uses ChatGPT Enterprise to research insurers, prepare proposals, and draft code for investment analysis. Early use by executives helped drive adoption.
news.source_text:
How Sumitomo Life’s leaders helped teams adopt ChatGPT Enterprise
Planning teams use ChatGPT to research overseas insurers and prepare proposals. Investment teams use it to draft code for risk analysis.
Results
80%+
Weekly usage rate for ChatGPT Enterprise
Results
524%
Average estimated ROI among employees using ChatGPT at least 101 times a month
ROI estimates are based on employee-reported time savings; overall estimated ROI is 203%.
When Sumitomo Life’s planning teams prepare proposals for senior management, ChatGPT Enterprise helps them review source material and organize their findings. They combine those findings with firsthand information and draw on their expertise to decide what to recommend. Teams in accounting and finance also use ChatGPT for research and analysis.
The Japanese life insurer’s executives and managers were among the first to use ChatGPT. Their example and the president’s encouragement helped more employees try it in their own work.
Sumitomo Life began using generative AI at work in 2023. At first, employees mainly asked questions in chat. As they tested general-purpose AI tools, ChatGPT stood out for its range. They could use deep research to explore a question across sources and bring ChatGPT into work they were already doing in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel.
In 2025, about 100 to 150 people, including executives and members of planning teams, piloted ChatGPT Business. In June 2026, the company moved to ChatGPT Enterprise. In planning a rollout to thousands of employees, the insurer weighed output quality, how well ChatGPT fit different kinds of work, and the security requirements of a financial institution.
Sumitomo Life worked with OpenAI to assess ChatGPT Enterprise against the insurer’s security standards. The review covered how Sumitomo Life could manage workspace access and feature permissions, along with OpenAI’s policy of excluding business data from model training by default. The insurer continues to decide how employees can use ChatGPT based on the information they handle and the systems they connect to.
Sumitomo Life’s investment teams use statistical analysis to forecast returns and assess risks such as price swings. ChatGPT helps analysts draft the code for that work, reducing the amount they need to write themselves.
Planning teams use ChatGPT to track developments at other Japanese insurers and find examples from overseas. They use that research to strengthen proposals for senior management.
Planning teams supplement public sources with firsthand information from people familiar with the work. They use projects in ChatGPT to keep the material together with related chats, files, and custom instructions.
Sumitomo Life’s president began using AI during the ChatGPT Business pilot. In management meetings and on the company’s internal portal, the president regularly encouraged employees to put it to work.
Kakeru Tateyama, a senior member of Sumitomo Life’s planning department, saw how that example shaped adoption.
news.summary: OpenAI’s ChatGPT Enterprise has been adopted by Sumitomo Life, boosting employee usage and ROI through AI-powered research and code drafting. The insurer’s leadership drove adoption and evaluated security fit, setting a model for enterprise AI integration.
news.enterprise_use: Check your organization’s ChatGPT Enterprise usage metrics and evaluate whether the tool’s integration with Google Workspace and Excel can automate repetitive research and code generation tasks. Inaction may mean missing productivity gains and competitive insights.

news.title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
news.summary_raw: Lenders don't want SpaceX shooting their collateral into orbit. What does that mean for space data centers writ large?
news.source_text:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.
But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.
That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.
However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.
Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.
Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.
That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry
news.summary: Space-based data centers are grappling with financing and logistical challenges, as lenders insist on not using chips for SpaceX’s orbital plans. The article highlights how chip resale values are declining and the uncertain economics of deploying compute in orbit, even as SpaceX pushes for reusable rockets.
news.enterprise_use: This news offers little immediate actionable insight for an IT engineer focused on Google Workspace, JumpCloud, Freshservice, and related tools. It does, however, underline the broader trend of cloud providers expanding into unconventional environments, suggesting a future where data locality and edge computing could shift infrastructure strategies.

news.title: Six AI-powered gadgets that could make your home office smarter
news.summary_raw: From notetakers to webcams, here are six AI-powered gadgets to upgrade your workspace.
news.source_text:
Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.
From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.
Flowtica Scribe Pen ($159)
If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.
The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.
You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.
The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.
Anker Soundcore Work ($159)
Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work, is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.
Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.
The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.
If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).
Logitech MX Keypad ($99)
Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.
The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.
Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($479)
Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.

news.title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://eli.thegreenplace.net/2017/clojure-the-perfect-language-to-expand-your-brain/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50585376
Points: 138
# Comments: 58
news.source_text:
I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis says:
A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing.
In this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a terrific language for this task. Whatever your background, it's almost guaranteed to affect the way you think about programming. It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain.
It's a Lisp!
First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things:
- Clojure is a dynamic language. No matter where you stand on the static vs. dynamic typing debate, knowing languages in both camps is important. Clojure has a kind of optional typing, but in essence it's dynamic.
- It promotes combinations of built-in data structures (lists, maps, vectors) over objects and has very good reasons for doing so.
- It promotes programming with higher-order functions. Some built-in features like reducers and transducers rely heavily on composing higher order functions for transforming other functions.
- It has uniform syntax with full Lisp-style macro support! This capability has proved to be very elusive for non-Lisp languages, and seeing some real macros in action is enlightening. Clojure has a whole Go-like CSP equivalent implemented using macros in core.async.
- It encourages REPL-based development, where functionality is built and testsed gradually from the bottom up in an interactive terminal.
Importantly, Clojure is a very modern Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.
I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight
news.summary: This 2017 Hacker News post discusses how learning Clojure can broaden a programmer’s perspective. The article highlights Clojure’s dynamic nature, macro system, and modern Lisp features but has no direct relevance to current IT infrastructure or AI tools.
